In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ability to discriminate individual letters does not necessarily imply that a child will be able to perceive individual letters in whole words.

the discrimination of printed letters does not guarantee the discrimination of whole printed words.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
letter discrimination is not sufficient for the discrimination of printed words, and that the discrimination of printed word stimuli requires additional learning.

children are not able to discriminate words that differ in only the first letter even though they can discriminate individual letters and even though they are able to discriminate words differing in the first letter if they are trained to discriminate the words using fading procedures.
the ability to discriminate individual printed letters is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the discrimination of printed words.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children who are learning to read must be taught to discriminate whole words.
the discrimination of printed words is more complex than the discrimination of individual letters and that this complexity may be a source of difficulty in beginning reading.

the discrimination of printed letters presented in isolation does not automatically entail accurate discrimination of printed letters within whole word stimuli, and that children must learn to discriminate printed words as a separate task.
